newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-TIMELINES - Today in History - Oct 3.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-TIMELINES - Today in History - Oct 3.

text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
English surveyor WILLIAM GOVETT, who discovered GOVETT's Leap (a waterfall) in the Blue Mountains of New South Wales, was born in 1807.
West Australian pastoralist and explorer EDWARD HOOLEY, who opened up areas of the Hamersley Ranges, was born in 1842.
Italian actress ELEANORA DUSE was born in 1859.
Australian journalist and author ADA HOLMAN was born in 1869. She was once asked how to handle a husband, and replied "Don't be a doormat".
American novelist, playwright and politician GORE VIDAL was born in 1925.
Australian actress and comedienne NOELINE BROWN, who became famous on television in the "Naked Vicar Show", was born in 1938.

American singer EDDIE COCHRAN was born in 1938. His first hits with the 'Cochran Brothers', a band formed with HANK COCHRAN (real name GARLAND PERRY) were "Summertime Blues" and "C'mon Everybody" in 1958. He died in England in a car crash.
American singer ALAN O'DAY, who wrote songs such as "Angie Baby" for Australia's HELEN REDDY and "Rock 'n' Roll Heaven" for the 'Righteous Brothers', was born in 1940.

American singer CHUBBY CHECKER (ERNEST EVANS), who had hits with "The Twist" (1960) and "Let's Twist Again" (1961), was born in 1941. He launched his singing career by performing imitations of FATS DOMINO, from whom he derived his name. CHUBBY - after FATS, and CHECKER - after DOMINO.
British singer/guitarist LINDSEY BUCKINGHAM, who worked in a duo with STEVIE NICKS before they joined 'Fleetwood Mac' in 1974, was born in 1947. He left the band in 1978.
American guitarist STEVIE RAY VAUGHAN, whose career was cut short when he died in a plane crash on the 27th of August, 1990, was born in 1954.
American drummer TOMMY LEE, who played with the heavy metal band 'Motley Crue', was born in 1962.
** EVENTS **
1226 : SAINT FRANCIS OF ASSISI, founder of the Franciscan
order who received the wounds of Christ (the stigmata) and endured great pain during the first two years of his life, died. 1863 : United States President ABRAHAM LINCOLN declared the

last day in November a national holiday, to be called "Thanksgiving". Thanksgiving originated in Massachusetts, where the first English colony was established. Following the first harvest in 1621, Governor WILLIAM BRADFORD called for a day of prayer and thanksgiving. This became a regular practice in other colonies from about 1630.
1867 : ELIAS HOWE, the man who patented the sewing
machine (earning him two million dollars) died.
1903 : The first publication of the Brisbane "Daily Mail"
hit the streets.
1905 : Australia's first Childrens' Court opened at
Ormond House in the Sydney suburb of Paddington. The court was established to deal exclusively with juvenile crime.
1906 : The "S.O.S" was established as an international
distress call.
1940 : British Prime Minister NEVILLE CHAMBERLAIN
resigned for 'health reasons'. WINSTON CHURCHILL would be elected as his replacement a week later.
1941 : The Australian Labor Party, under JOHN CURTIN, was
asked to form a government after the ARTHUR FADDEN government was defeated in a no-confidence motion.
1941 : The movie "The Maltese Falcon" premiered in New
York, starring HUMPHREY BOGART.
1952 : The first British atomic weapon was exploded off

the Monte Bello Islands, north west of Australia. The test was designed to assess the effect of an atomic bomb exploding in a harbour. The device was detonated aboard the 1,370 ton frigate "HMS PLYM", vapourizing the vessel except for a few fragments which landed on nearby islands. The force of the blast was felt 104 kilometres away.
1959 : Post codes were introduced in Britain.
1967 : American folk musician WOODY GUTHRIE died. He had
suffered from an inherited nerve disease Huntington's chorea. He was born on the 14th of July, 1912.
1967 : Popular British conductor SIR MALCOLM SARGENT
died.
1968 : The Transport Regulation Board in Melbourne
approved the licensing of women taxi drivers.
1972 : United States President RICHARD NIXON and Soviet
Foreign Minister ANDREI GROMYKO signed the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty (SALT), limiting the two countries to having 200 anti-ballistic missiles.
1983 : Royal Perth Yacht Club Commodore PETER DALZIELL
arrived home with the America's Cup. "Australia II" skippered by JOHN BERTRAND had won the Cup on the 26th of September.
1984 : TIM MACARTNEY-SNAPE and GREG MORTIMER became the

first Australians to reach the 8,848-metre summit of Mount Everest. Just a week later, there was tragedy for a separate Australian attempt on the peak, led by SIR EDMUND HILLARY's son PETER. Two climbers died in a fall during a final assault on the mountain's steep west ridge.
1991 : The British Director of Public Prosecutions, SIR

ALLAN GREEN QC, resigned after being stopped by police for alleged curb crawling - (attempting to procure prostitutes from the street). Outspoken prostitute LINDI ST CLAIR had recently urged SIR ALLAN to legalise prostitution.
